name: Earthing therapy

card.summary: Earthing is the practice of making skin contact with the ground, barefoot or via conductive mats, which proponents say calms inflammation, improves sleep and supports healthier-looking skin.
card.note: Research is small and largely produced by people tied to a company selling grounding products.

quick.overview:
Earthing, also called grounding, is the idea that touching the Earth's surface, by walking barefoot on grass, sand or soil or by using conductive mats, sheets or patches, lets the body take up free electrons from the ground. Proponents say this settles inflammation and stress responses, which they connect to better sleep, less soreness and a calmer-looking complexion.

In appearance terms the chain runs from better sleep and lower inflammation to recovery and skin condition. A 2012 review by researchers affiliated with an earthing company summarises small pilot studies on pain, sleep and muscle soreness. Mainstream skeptics describe the field as pseudoscience and criticise the studies' size and sponsorship.
quick.how: Practitioners go barefoot outdoors on grass, soil, sand or concrete for a period each day, or use conductive mats, bedsheets, bands or patches connected to a grounded wall outlet or ground rod. Routines are usually folded into sleep, desk work or training recovery. Followers report noticing changes in sleep and soreness over days to weeks.
quick.risks: Barefoot outdoor contact carries the ordinary risks of cuts, infection and parasites depending on the ground. Indoor mats rely on a grounded outlet, and electrical safety guidance applies to anything plugged into mains. Medical commentators say the health claims are not established, so earthing is not presented as a substitute for treatment of any condition.

lead: Earthing therapy, also called grounding, is an alternative-health practice in which a person keeps bare skin in contact with the Earth's surface, or with a conductive product wired to ground, on the theory that surface electrons from the Earth benefit the body.[1][2]

In looksmaxxing and wellness circles the appeal is indirect: proponents link earthing to deeper sleep, less muscle soreness and lower inflammation, which in turn support training recovery and a rested, clearer-looking face and skin.[1]

A 2012 review in the Journal of Environmental and Public Health summarised small pilot studies on sleep, pain, cortisol rhythm and heart rate variability, and proposed that electrons from the ground may neutralise reactive oxygen species at sites of inflammation.[1] Its authors have financial ties to the company that sponsored the work, and skeptics such as Steven Novella and Harriet Hall have criticised the research.[2]

chain: Barefoot or mat contact with ground
Claimed lower inflammation and better sleep
Better recovery and a rested complexion
angle.text: People who practise earthing use barefoot time outdoors or grounded sheets and mats hoping for better sleep and less inflammation. They tie those to recovery from training and to a fresher, calmer-looking skin appearance.

infobox: Barefoot contact; conductive mats, sheets, bands, patches
Transfer of Earth surface electrons to the body

paras: Practitioners aim for direct electrical contact between the skin and the ground. Outdoors this means barefoot standing or walking on grass, sand, soil or wet concrete; indoors it means conductive sheets, mats or patches connected by a cable to the grounding port of a wall outlet or to a rod in the earth.[1]

Proponents say modern footwear and insulated flooring cut people off from this contact, and that restoring it stabilises the body's electrical environment. They associate this with inflammation, ageing, sleep and a range of chronic conditions.[2]

The 2012 review proposes that free electrons from the Earth's surface act as antioxidants, neutralising reactive oxygen species at inflammatory sites. It presents this as a plausible mechanism rather than an established one and says more study is needed in areas such as thyroid function.[1]

Reported effects in the cited pilot studies include less pain, better sleep including a more normal day-night cortisol pattern, a shift from sympathetic toward parasympathetic activity, reduced red blood cell aggregation, and a muted white-cell response and less pain after delayed-onset muscle soreness in grounded men.[1]
Wider claims made by promoters cover heart disease, diabetes, arthritis, autoimmune disorders, depression and other conditions.[2]

Published human work consists mostly of small pilot studies, several with 8 to 12 participants, with outcomes such as sleep and pain often self-reported.[1] Three authors of the 2012 review are independent contractors for Earthx Inc., the company that sponsored the research, and hold shares in it.[1]

Skeptical commentators describe earthing as pseudoscience. Neurologist Steven Novella wrote that such studies are designed to generate false positives, and Harriet Hall and Brian Dunning have also published critiques.[2]

Earthing is mentioned in wellness-oriented corners of the community as a free or low-cost addition to sleep and recovery routines, alongside sunlight and breathwork. It generally appears as a background habit rather than a core protocol.

timeline.event: Chevalier, Sinatra, Oschman and colleagues publish an earthing review in the Journal of Environmental and Public Health.[1]

lore.intro: Earthing is discussed as a low-effort recovery and sleep habit and a claimed anti-inflammatory for skin.[1]

claims.believers: Proponents say ground electrons neutralise free radicals at inflamed sites and point to a muscle-soreness pilot study.[1]
claims.experts: The mechanism is described by the review's own authors as plausible rather than established, and critics note small samples and sponsor ties.[1][2]

claims.believers: Users and promoters report easier, deeper sleep with grounded sheets.[1]
claims.experts: The supporting data are small pilot studies relying partly on self-report.[1]

claims.believers: Promoters link it to heart disease, diabetes, arthritis and more.[2]
claims.experts: Skeptics and the medical community regard these claims as pseudoscience.[2]
